meta.title: The Bridge Course
meta.subtitle: From Globe to Flat Map — The Complete Classification Guide
meta.description: An interactive, in-depth guide to understanding map projection classification. Covers the full GIS coordinate system hierarchy, the three axes of projection classification (surface family × preserved property × aspect), the ESRI/Snyder taxonomy, decision flowcharts, and how to use this portal effectively.

ESRI ArcGIS Pro — Coordinate Systems & Map Projections Documentation

cards.title: The Shelf
cards.description: Browse all 24 projections as filterable cards. Filter by surface family (cylindrical, conic, azimuthal…) or preserved property (conformal, equal-area…). Click any card to see a live d3-geo rendered map, metadata, and distortion notes.

cards.title: Mix Station
cards.description: The recipe engine. Tell the app what you're mapping, what matters most (area? shape? direction?), where it is, and what it's for. The engine scores all 24 projections and serves you a verdict: Great, Workable, Clashing, or Impossible — with suggested alternatives.

cards.title: Distortion Lab
cards.description: Visualize Tissot's Indicatrix — small geodesic circles that deform into ellipses showing exactly where and how a projection distorts. Toggle tangent/secant case, change aspect (normal/transverse/oblique), and slide the azimuthal perspective continuum from Gnomonic → Stereographic → Satellite → Orthographic.

cards.title: Bridge Course (You Are Here)
cards.description: The conceptual backbone. Interactive family trees, classification charts, glossary, and zoom-out diagrams that show how every projection in this portal fits into the bigger GIS picture — from coordinate systems all the way down to individual projection parameters.

steps.title: Start here in the Bridge Course
steps.detail: Read Chapter 1 (Coordinate Systems) and Chapter 2 (The Three Axes) to build the mental model.

steps.title: Browse the Shelf
steps.detail: Open 'The Shelf' tab and explore projections by family. Click into a few cards — the metadata and distortion notes will make much more sense now.

steps.title: Try the Mix Station
steps.detail: Experiment with different mapping goals. Watch how changing 'area matters most' vs 'shape matters most' shifts the verdict. The rules connect directly to Chapter 2's classification.

steps.title: Inspect in the Distortion Lab
steps.detail: Pick a projection and see Tissot circles deform in real time. Compare a conformal projection (circles stay circular) to an equal-area one (circles become ellipses but maintain area).

steps.title: Return to the Bridge Course
steps.detail: Re-read the Decision Flowchart (Chapter 4) with fresh eyes. You'll now have the visual intuition to pick the right projection for any mapping task.

sections.title: The GIS Coordinate System Hierarchy
sections.description: Every map in GIS starts with a coordinate system. Before you can project (flatten) the Earth, you must first define where things are on the 3D globe. This hierarchy shows how all the pieces fit together — from the broadest category down to specific parameters.

children.label: Horizontal Coordinate Systems (HCS)
children.description: Define position across the Earth's surface (latitude/longitude or x/y)

children.label: Geographic Coordinate System (GCS)
children.description: 3D angular reference on the ellipsoid. Uses latitude & longitude in degrees.

children.label: Datum
children.description: Defines the size/shape of the ellipsoid and its position relative to the Earth (e.g., WGS 84, NAD 83).

children.label: Spheroid / Ellipsoid
children.description: Mathematical model of the Earth's shape. Not a perfect sphere — slightly flattened at the poles (e.g., WGS 84 ellipsoid, GRS 1980).

children.label: Angular Unit
children.description: The unit for measuring angles — almost always decimal degrees.

children.label: Prime Meridian
children.description: The zero line of longitude. Usually Greenwich (0°), but historically varied.

children.label: Projected Coordinate System (PCS)
children.description: 2D flat reference. Always inherits a GCS, then adds a map projection + parameters.

children.label: Inherits a GCS
children.description: Every PCS is built on top of a GCS. You can't project without first fixing a datum, ellipsoid, and prime meridian.

children.label: Map Projection
children.description: The mathematical algorithm that converts 3D angular coordinates to 2D planar coordinates. This is the core topic of this portal.

children.label: Classified by Developable Surface
children.description: Cylindrical, Conic, Azimuthal, Pseudocylindrical, Compromise

children.label: Classified by Preserved Property
children.description: Conformal, Equal-Area, Equidistant, True-Direction, Compromise

children.label: Classified by Aspect
children.description: Normal, Transverse, Oblique

children.label: Projection Parameters
children.description: Settings like standard parallels, central meridian, false easting/northing, scale factor.

children.label: Linear Unit
children.description: The unit for measuring on the flat map — meters, feet, etc.

children.label: Vertical Coordinate Systems (VCS)
children.description: Define height/elevation above a reference surface

children.label: Vertical Datum
children.description: The reference surface for measuring height.

children.label: Ellipsoidal (Geometric)
children.description: Height above the mathematical ellipsoid. Used by GPS directly.

children.label: Gravity-Related (Geoid)
children.description: Height above mean sea level (geoid). Used for most practical elevation data (e.g., EGM96, NAVD 88).

children.label: Vertical Shift
children.description: Transformation between vertical datums.

children.label: Direction
children.description: Up or Down — whether the shift adds or subtracts elevation.

children.label: Linear Unit
children.description: Meters, feet, etc.

sections.title: The Key Insight
sections.text: A Projected Coordinate System (PCS) = Geographic Coordinate System (GCS) + Map Projection + Parameters. You can never project without first fixing a datum and ellipsoid. That's why the GCS arrow feeds into the PCS in every hierarchy diagram — it's not optional, it's inherited.

sections.title: GCS vs. PCS — When to Use Which
rows: Global data storage, GPS, web services (WGS 84)
Any measurement (area, distance), local maps, analysis
Always present — you choose which kind

sections.title: Three Independent Dimensions
sections.text: Every map projection can be classified along three independent axes: (1) by surface family — the geometric shape used to 'catch' the projected light, (2) by preserved property — what geometric truth the projection protects, and (3) by aspect — how the projection surface is oriented relative to the Earth's axis. These three axes are independent: any combination is theoretically possible, though not all are commonly used.

sections.title: Axis 1 — Surface Family (Developable Surface)
sections.description: The geometric shape onto which the globe is projected. Imagine shining a light from the center of a transparent globe onto a nearby surface — the shadow of the continents is your map.

cards.name: Cylindrical
cards.graticule: Parallels and meridians form a perpendicular grid of straight lines (in normal aspect)
cards.bestFor: Navigation, web maps, narrow N–S strips
cards.weakness: Extreme distortion near poles in normal aspect

cards.name: Conic
cards.graticule: Meridians radiate from a point; parallels are concentric arcs
cards.bestFor: Mid-latitude regions with east–west extent (US, Europe, Russia)
cards.weakness: Cannot show the whole world; distortion grows away from standard parallels

cards.name: Azimuthal (Planar)
cards.surface: Flat plane touching the globe at one point
cards.graticule: Meridians radiate from center; parallels are concentric circles (polar aspect)
cards.bestFor: Polar regions, single-city distance maps, hemisphere views
cards.weakness: Only the center point has zero distortion; distortion increases outward in all directions

cards.name: Pseudocylindrical
cards.surface: No literal geometric surface — parallels are straight, meridians curve
cards.graticule: Parallels are straight horizontal lines, but meridians curve toward the poles
cards.bestFor: Whole-world thematic maps showing area distributions
cards.weakness: Shape distortion at edges/poles; no literal 'unwrapping' — purely mathematical

cards.name: Compromise / Miscellaneous
cards.surface: No single developable surface — designed by balancing distortions mathematically
cards.graticule: Varies — often curved meridians, curved or straight parallels
cards.bestFor: General-reference world maps, atlases, wall maps
cards.weakness: Doesn't perfectly preserve any single property — a little of everything is distorted

sections.title: Axis 2 — Preserved Property (What the Projection Protects)
sections.description: No flat map can preserve everything — each projection must choose what to protect. This is the fundamental trade-off of cartography.
sections.tradeoff: It is mathematically impossible for a flat map to simultaneously preserve area AND angles everywhere. A conformal map will exaggerate areas; an equal-area map will distort shapes. This is a theorem, not a limitation of technology.

properties.name: Conformal (Orthomorphic)
properties.preserves: Local angles and shapes of small features
properties.distorts: Area — often severely near poles or map edges
properties.howToSpot: Tissot circles remain perfect circles (but grow larger away from the standard lines)

properties.name: Equal-Area (Equivalent)
properties.preserves: Area — any region on the map has the correct proportional area relative to the globe
properties.distorts: Shape and angle — features may be stretched, compressed, or sheared
properties.howToSpot: Tissot ellipses all have the same area (but shapes vary — some are squished, some stretched)
useCases: Any time 'how much' matters more than 'what shape'

properties.name: Equidistant
properties.preserves: True distance from one point (or along specific lines)
properties.distorts: Everything else, away from those specific lines or points
properties.howToSpot: Distances measured from the center point (or along meridians) are correct; all others are not

properties.name: True-Direction (Azimuthal)
properties.preserves: True compass bearing (azimuth) from the center point to every other point
properties.distorts: Distance, area, and shape away from center
properties.howToSpot: A straight line from the center of the map to any point shows the true great-circle direction
keyProjections: Azimuthal Equidistant (also preserves distance from center)

properties.name: Compromise (Aphylactic)
properties.preserves: A pleasant overall balance — nothing perfectly, but everything reasonably
properties.distorts: A little of everything, on purpose
properties.howToSpot: Tissot ellipses vary in both size and shape, but nothing is extreme

sections.title: Axis 3 — Aspect (Orientation of the Projection Surface)
sections.description: The aspect describes how the projection surface (cylinder, cone, or plane) is oriented relative to the Earth's polar axis. Changing the aspect rotates where distortion is minimized.

aspects.name: Normal (Equatorial)
aspects.description: The axis of the projection surface aligns with the Earth's polar axis. For a cylinder: tangent at the equator. For a cone: axis coincides with Earth's axis. For a plane: centered on a pole.
aspects.example: Mercator (normal cylindrical) — equator is the line of zero distortion

aspects.name: Transverse
aspects.description: The axis of the projection surface is rotated 90° — perpendicular to the Earth's polar axis. For a cylinder: tangent along a meridian instead of the equator.
aspects.bestFor: Narrow north–south strips. This is exactly what UTM does — it wraps a transverse cylinder around each 6°-wide meridional zone.
aspects.example: Transverse Mercator / UTM — each zone's central meridian is the line of zero distortion

aspects.name: Oblique
aspects.description: The axis is tilted at any angle between normal and transverse. The projection surface touches the globe along a great circle that is neither the equator nor a meridian.
aspects.bestFor: Regions that don't align with the equator or a meridian — e.g., Italy, Japan, New Zealand, a trans-oceanic flight path
aspects.example: Oblique Mercator — used for areas like Alaska's panhandle or the Strait of Malacca

sections.description: Any projection can be located in this 3D space: Surface × Property × Aspect. Here's a simplified 2D slice showing Surface Family × Preserved Property, with example projections in each cell.

cells.note: By definition, compromises don't perfectly preserve any property

sections.title: Tangent vs. Secant Case
sections.description: Every surface family has two 'cases' — how the projection surface touches the globe. This determines where distortion is zero.

pairs.name: Tangent
pairs.description: The surface touches the globe along one line (or at one point). Distortion is zero only along that line/point and increases outward.
pairs.details: Cylinder tangent at equator → 1 standard parallel at 0°. Cone tangent at 45°N → 1 standard parallel. Plane tangent at pole → 1 contact point.

pairs.name: Secant
pairs.description: The surface cuts through the globe along two lines. Distortion is zero along both lines, resulting in less overall distortion across the mapped region.
pairs.details: Cylinder secant at 30°N & 30°S → 2 standard parallels. Cone secant at 33°N & 45°N → 2 standard parallels (e.g., Albers for CONUS). This is the real-world default — most practical projections use secant case.

sections.title: Projection Light Source (for Azimuthal family)
sections.description: For azimuthal projections, the location of the 'light source' determines the mathematical character of the projection.

items.name: Gnomonic
items.special: Every great circle appears as a straight line — invaluable for plotting shortest paths. Severe distortion beyond ~60° from center.

items.name: Stereographic
items.source: Antipodal point (opposite side of the globe)
items.special: Conformal — preserves angles everywhere. Can show an entire hemisphere.

items.name: Orthographic
items.special: Looks like viewing a globe from deep space. Only the visible hemisphere is shown.

items.truth: UTM is a Transverse Mercator variant — it's conformal (preserves angles), not equal-area. It inherits Mercator's angle-preserving property, just rotated so the tangent line runs along a meridian instead of the equator.

Mercator makes high-latitude areas look too BIG (Greenland appears as large as Africa). Africa is actually 14× larger than Greenland. Mercator is conformal — it exaggerates area at high latitudes to preserve angles.
There is no universal best projection. Each projection is a deliberate trade-off. The 'best' depends entirely on your map's purpose, extent, and location. That's why this portal has a Mix Station.

The 'developable surface' (cylinder, cone, plane) is a conceptual/pedagogical model, not a physical process. Most projections are defined by mathematical formulas. The surface metaphor helps you understand the pattern of distortion, but the math doesn't require a literal cone or cylinder.

WGS 84 (EPSG:4326) is a Geographic Coordinate System — it defines the datum and ellipsoid. It's unprojected. Data in WGS 84 is in degrees of latitude/longitude on the 3D ellipsoid. To show it on a flat screen, your software applies a projection (often Plate Carrée or Web Mercator) on the fly.

items.myth: Equal-area and equidistant mean the same thing
items.truth: They are completely different properties. Equal-area preserves the relative size of regions. Equidistant preserves true distance from a specific point or along specific lines. A map can be one or the other, but not both everywhere.

terms.definition: A reference framework that defines the size and shape of the Earth's ellipsoid and its position relative to the Earth's center. Examples: WGS 84, NAD 83, ED 50.
A mathematical surface approximating the Earth's shape. Slightly flattened at the poles. Different datums may use different ellipsoids.

A unique integer identifier for a specific coordinate system, maintained by the European Petroleum Survey Group (now IOGP). Example: EPSG:4326 = WGS 84 (geographic), EPSG:3857 = Web Mercator (projected).
The grid of parallels (latitude lines) and meridians (longitude lines) drawn on a map.
The largest circle that can be drawn on a sphere, representing the shortest path between two points on the globe.
A systematic mathematical transformation that converts locations on the 3D Earth surface to positions on a 2D flat surface (a map).
The line(s) where the projection surface touches (tangent) or cuts through (secant) the globe. Distortion is zero along these lines.

A visualization tool: infinitely small circles on the globe are projected onto the map, showing how the projection distorts area, shape, and angles at each point. On a conformal map, they stay circular (but vary in size). On an equal-area map, they all have the same area (but may be stretched).
Well-Known ID — ESRI's equivalent of EPSG codes for identifying coordinate systems.
The ability of GIS software to temporarily reproject layers from their native coordinate system into the map frame's coordinate system for display, without permanently altering the source data.
The meridian at the center of a map projection, often the line of zero distortion for cylindrical projections.
Constants added to projected x/y coordinates to avoid negative values. UTM adds 500,000m false easting so all coordinates in a zone are positive.
A geometric shape (cylinder, cone, plane) that can be 'unrolled' into a flat surface without stretching. The conceptual basis for classifying projection families.
A map property that preserves local angles and shapes. Meridians and parallels cross at right angles everywhere.
A map property that preserves the proportional area of regions. A country that is 2% of the world on the globe is 2% of the world on the map.
Neither conformal nor equal-area — a compromise projection that balances multiple types of distortion.
